playa-del-duque.name: Playa del Duque
playa-del-duque.alt: The striped beach houses on the golden sand of Playa del Duque
playa-del-duque.tagline: The most upmarket stretch of sand in the south, and the one people picture when they picture Costa Adeje.
playa-del-duque.intro: Playa del Duque is where Costa Adeje puts on its best clothes. A Blue Flag crescent of golden sand backed by the Bahía del Duque resort and a run of designer shops, it is calmer and considerably smarter than the beaches further along the coast, and the water is usually gentle enough for a proper swim.
playa-del-duque.see: The beach itself is the attraction: soft imported sand, sun loungers and parasols for rent at roughly ten to fifteen euros, and a set of striped wooden beach houses that have become the postcard image of the resort. The promenade behind it runs north towards La Caleta and south towards Fañabé, so a stroll in either direction is easy. Plaza del Duque, a short walk inland, is the island's most upmarket shopping centre, and La Torre del Mirador sits above the sand for a long lunch with a view.
playa-del-duque.getting: It is a twenty to twenty-five minute drive from Tenerife South Airport along the TF-1, and walkable from most of Costa Adeje along the seafront promenade. TITSA buses serve Costa Adeje from Los Cristianos and Playa de las Américas for a couple of euros, and parking near the beach fills early in peak season.
playa-del-duque.tips: Mornings are noticeably quieter, and the light is better for photographs before the sun climbs. Sunbed rental is not cheap here compared with Los Cristianos, so bring a towel if you are counting euros. The UV is high year-round, even in winter, and the sea breeze hides how fast you are burning.
highlights: Designer shopping at Plaza del Duque
faq: Is Playa del Duque a good beach for families?

Yes. The sand is soft, the water is usually calm and there are lifeguards in season, plus plenty of facilities behind the beach. Playa de las Vistas in Los Cristianos is even more sheltered if you have very small children.
Is the sand at Playa del Duque natural?
Like several southern beaches, the golden sand is imported rather than the island's native volcanic black. It is one reason this stretch looks so different from the beaches of the north and west.
How much are sunbeds at Playa del Duque?
Expect roughly ten to fifteen euros for a lounger and parasol, which is at the higher end for the island. Prices vary by operator and season.

playa-de-las-vistas.name: Playa de las Vistas
playa-de-las-vistas.alt: Playa de las Vistas beach in Los Cristianos
playa-de-las-vistas.tagline: The safest, calmest big beach in the south, and the one to choose with small children.
playa-de-las-vistas.intro: Playa de las Vistas stretches for over a kilometre between Los Cristianos and Playa de las Américas, and it is the most family-friendly beach on this coast. Breakwaters keep the water flat, the imported golden sand shelves gently, and everything you need is within a few steps of the promenade behind it.
playa-de-las-vistas.see: Swimming is the point here: the sheltered water is calm enough for children and weak swimmers, and there are lifeguards through the season. The beach has good accessibility, including ramps and assisted bathing services. Behind it, the promenade runs into the old town of Los Cristianos in one direction, with the working harbour and its fish restaurants at the far end, and towards Las Américas in the other.
playa-de-las-vistas.getting: Fifteen to twenty minutes from Tenerife South Airport along the TF-1. The beach sits between the two resorts, so it is walkable from either. TITSA buses stop nearby, and the whole seafront from Los Cristianos to Costa Adeje is flat and easy on foot or with a pushchair.
playa-de-las-vistas.tips: The Los Cristianos end is generally quieter than the Las Américas end. It is one of the better-value spots on the coast for eating, since the old town behind it has plenty of local restaurants a street or two back from the sand. Sunday mornings bring a market near the harbour.
faq: Is Playa de las Vistas safe for swimming?
It is among the safest big beaches in Tenerife. Breakwaters keep the water calm and there are lifeguards in season. Always follow the flags, as Atlantic conditions can still change.
Is Playa de las Vistas better than Playa del Duque?
For families and swimming, generally yes: it is calmer and cheaper. Playa del Duque is smarter and quieter, with better facilities at the upmarket end.

la-caleta.name: La Caleta
la-caleta.alt: White houses along the seafront at La Caleta
la-caleta.tagline: A former fishing hamlet at the quiet end of Costa Adeje, and the best place on the island to eat fish by the water.
la-caleta.intro: La Caleta sits at the northern edge of Costa Adeje, where the resorts run out and the coast turns rocky. It was a fishing village and still trades on it: a short seafront lined with fish restaurants, a small rocky bay, and a pace that drops noticeably the moment you arrive. There is no nightlife to speak of, which is exactly why people come.
la-caleta.see: Eating is the main event. The seafront restaurants serve the day's catch with papas arrugadas and mojo, and a table over the water at lunch, looking across to La Gomera, is one of the south's better hours. The village also holds several Michelin-starred kitchens in and around the Royal Hideaway Corales complex, including the two-starred El Rincón de Juan Carlos. Beyond the food, there is a small bay for a dip, a coastal path towards Playa del Duque, and not a great deal else.
la-caleta.getting: About twenty-five minutes from Tenerife South Airport, at the end of the Costa Adeje seafront. You can walk along the promenade from Playa del Duque in roughly half an hour, or drive and park in the village, which gets tight at weekends and in the evening.
la-caleta.tips: Book a table if you want a seafront spot at dinner, especially at weekends when locals drive down from inland. Lunch is the better value and the better light. Prices here are at the higher end for the island, and the bay is rocky rather than sandy, so bring water shoes if you plan to swim.
faq: Is La Caleta worth visiting?
For a meal, yes. It has the best concentration of seafront fish restaurants in the south and a far calmer atmosphere than the resorts. It is not a beach destination, as the bay is small and rocky.
Do you need to book restaurants in La Caleta?
For dinner and at weekends, yes. The seafront tables are the ones people want and they go early.

siam-park.name: Siam Park
siam-park.alt: Siam Park water park in Costa Adeje
siam-park.tagline: Repeatedly voted the world's best water park, and the south's single strongest attraction.
siam-park.intro: Siam Park sits on the hillside above Costa Adeje, an elaborately Thai-themed water park that has topped traveller polls for years. It is bigger, cleaner and better landscaped than the genre usually manages, and it comfortably fills a full day.
siam-park.see: The headline ride is the Tower of Power, a near-vertical drop that fires you through a tube running inside a shark aquarium. Beyond it there is the Dragon, the Singha rollercoaster-style slide, a wave pool that produces genuinely large waves, the Mai Thai River lazy river, and the Lost City play area for younger children. Siam Beach gives you white sand and loungers when you have had enough of the queues.
siam-park.getting: A short drive above Costa Adeje, roughly twenty minutes from Tenerife South Airport, with a free shuttle bus looping the main southern resorts. Parking is available on site.
siam-park.tips: Go early: the queues build sharply from late morning and the park is at its best in the first two hours. In peak season the fast-pass upgrade genuinely saves time rather than just money. Height restrictions apply on the bigger rides, so check before promising anything to a small child. Bring a towel and expect to pay for lockers.
faq: How much does Siam Park cost?
An adult day ticket starts at around forty euros, with children cheaper and a twin ticket with Loro Parque at roughly seventy. Booking online is normally cheaper than at the gate.
Is Siam Park worth it?
For most visitors, yes. It is the strongest single attraction in the south and the standard is unusually high. Go early and consider the fast pass in peak season.
siam-park.title: Siam Park, Tenerife — Visitor Guide & Tips

playa-de-las-teresitas.name: Playa de las Teresitas
playa-de-las-teresitas.alt: The golden crescent of Playa de las Teresitas
playa-de-las-teresitas.tagline: A golden crescent of Saharan sand a short drive from the capital, and arguably the prettiest big beach on the island.
playa-de-las-teresitas.intro: Playa de las Teresitas curves for over a kilometre beside the fishing village of San Andrés, north-east of Santa Cruz. The golden sand was shipped in from the Sahara in the early 1970s and a breakwater keeps the water flat, which makes it both beautiful and unusually calm for this coast. What it is not is a resort: locals outnumber tourists most weekends, and that is its charm.
playa-de-las-teresitas.see: Swimming and lying still, mostly. Palms line the back of the beach, there are showers and beach bars, and parking behind the sand is free. San Andrés at the near end is a working fishing village with a run of good fish restaurants, and the road onwards leads into the Anaga mountains, so the beach pairs naturally with a drive into the hills.
playa-de-las-teresitas.getting: Roughly fifteen minutes north-east of Santa Cruz by car or local bus. From the southern resorts allow around an hour on the TF-1, or take the 110 or 111 express bus to Santa Cruz and continue locally.
playa-de-las-teresitas.tips: Sunny weekends fill it with local families, which is part of the experience but means arriving early for a parking space. It is noticeably more sheltered than the wild Anaga beaches further round the coast, so it suits families where Benijo does not. Combine it with lunch in San Andrés and an afternoon in Anaga.
faq: Is the sand at Las Teresitas imported?
Yes. The golden sand was brought from the Sahara in the early 1970s. The island's own beaches on this coast are volcanic black.
Can you swim at Playa de las Teresitas?
Yes, and it is one of the calmer big beaches on the island thanks to the breakwater that shelters it.

playa-de-benijo.name: Playa de Benijo
playa-de-benijo.alt: The wild Anaga coastline at Playa de Benijo
playa-de-benijo.tagline: Black sand, jagged rock stacks and serious Atlantic surf at the end of the Anaga road.
playa-de-benijo.intro: Playa de Benijo sits at the far end of the Anaga coast road, where the mountains fall straight into the ocean. Black volcanic sand, offshore rock stacks and heavy surf make it the most photographed beach on the island, and one of the least suitable for a casual swim.
playa-de-benijo.see: The view is the reason to come, particularly late in the day when the sun drops behind the rocks. A stepped path leads down from the road to the sand. Walkers can continue along the coast towards El Draguillo, and the restaurants above the beach serve fresh fish with one of the better dining views in Tenerife. At low tide the beach opens out considerably.
playa-de-benijo.getting: About an hour from Santa Cruz on the TF-12 and TF-134 through Anaga, a spectacular but relentlessly winding drive. There is no easy bus, so a car or an organised tour is realistic. Parking at the end of the road is very limited and fills at weekends.
playa-de-benijo.tips: Swim with great caution or not at all: the Atlantic here has strong currents and there are no lifeguards. Go on a weekday if you can, and allow far longer for the drive than the distance suggests. Anyone prone to car sickness should sit in the front. Mist on the ridge is normal even when the coast is sunny.
highlights: Black sand and offshore rock stacks
Fresh fish with a view above the beach
faq: Can you swim at Playa de Benijo?
Only with great caution. The surf is strong, there are currents and no lifeguards. Most visitors come for the view and the walk rather than to swim.
How do you get to Benijo without a car?
Buses into Anaga are sparse and slow. Most visitors drive or join a guided Anaga tour from the south or from Santa Cruz.

masca.name: Masca
masca.tagline: A hamlet clinging to a ridge deep in the Teno mountains, at the head of Tenerife's most dramatic gorge.
masca.intro: Masca is a scatter of houses on a knife-edge ridge, surrounded by ravines that drop towards the sea. It is the island's most photographed village and the starting point of the Barranco de Masca hike, and getting there is half the story: the road in is one of the most demanding scenic drives in Europe.
masca.see: The village itself takes an hour: a church, a few terraces, several cafés with staggering views, and paths that lead a short way out onto the ridge for the classic photograph. The serious attraction is the gorge below, a steep one-way descent to a hidden cove, which is now strictly regulated and must be booked in advance. Most visitors simply come for the drive, the view and lunch.
masca.getting: The TF-436 from Santiago del Teide is about twenty minutes and roughly five kilometres of hairpins, barely two cars wide in places, with steep drops and coaches coming the other way. Confident drivers only, and go early. Parking in the village is very limited. Hikers doing the gorge must arrive on the TITSA 355 bus, as private cars are not permitted for them.
masca.tips: Early morning and late afternoon are both quieter and better lit than the middle of the day, when tour coaches arrive. If the drive sounds like too much, an organised tour or a boat trip from Los Gigantes to Masca bay gives you the scenery without the hairpins.
highlights: Gateway to the Barranco de Masca
One of Europe's great scenic drives
Cafés with a drop beneath them
faq: Is the road to Masca dangerous?
It is narrow and full of hairpins with steep drops, and it demands confidence and full attention, but it is well surfaced. Go early, drive slowly and expect to meet coaches.
Do you need to book to visit Masca village?
No, the village is free to visit. Only the gorge hike below it requires a paid permit and arrival by the official bus.
masca.title: Masca, Tenerife — Village, Drive & Gorge Guide

los-gigantes.name: Los Gigantes
los-gigantes.tagline: Sheer cliffs up to about 500 metres falling straight into the Atlantic, best seen from the water.
los-gigantes.intro: The Acantilados de los Gigantes, the Cliffs of the Giants, are the most imposing piece of coastline in Tenerife. The resort town of the same name sits at their foot, built on steep streets that tumble down to a small marina tucked right against the cliff wall.
los-gigantes.see: The cliffs are the attraction, and they are far more impressive from the sea than from land. Boat trips leave the marina for two to three hours beneath the rock faces, usually with a swim stop at Masca bay, and pilot whales and dolphins are commonly seen on the way. Kayak and snorkel trips run along the same coast. On land, the Mirador de Archipenque above town gives the classic view, and Playa de los Guíos is a small black-sand beach beside the marina.
los-gigantes.getting: Roughly twenty-five to thirty-five minutes from Costa Adeje via the TF-1 and TF-47, and about forty-five minutes from Tenerife South Airport. Parking in the town is genuinely tight, so use the car parks above and walk down.
los-gigantes.tips: Morning boat trips usually have calmer water. The whole coast faces west, which makes this one of the best places on the island for sunset, either from the Mirador de Archipenque or from an evening sailing. Treat the Crab Island tidal pool north of the marina with real caution and obey closures, as there have been fatalities there.
highlights: Some of the island's best sunsets
faq: What is the best way to see the Los Gigantes cliffs?
From the water. Boat trips from the marina run for two to three hours from around thirty euros and often include a swim stop and dolphin sightings.
Is Los Gigantes a good base for a holiday?
It suits couples, walkers and anyone wanting quiet with dramatic scenery. There is no nightlife strip, and beaches here are small and black-sand.
los-gigantes.title: Los Gigantes, Tenerife — Cliffs & Boat Trips

garachico.name: Garachico
garachico.alt: The natural rock pools of El Caletón at Garachico
garachico.tagline: The north's prettiest small town, with natural rock pools made by the lava that destroyed its harbour.
garachico.intro: Garachico was the richest port in Tenerife until a volcanic eruption in 1706 poured lava through the town and filled the harbour. What was a catastrophe left behind El Caletón, a set of natural pools in the cooled lava that people now swim in, and a compact old town of cobbled lanes, convents and plazas that many visitors rate their favourite on the island.
garachico.see: The rock pools are the draw: a series of channels and basins in the black lava, swimmable on calm days and closed when the swell is up. The old town behind them rewards an hour of wandering, and there are two of the island's loveliest historic hotels here. It is a half day at minimum, and genuinely lovely to stay overnight once the day-trippers have gone.
garachico.getting: About an hour and a half from the southern resorts, or twenty-five minutes west of Puerto de la Cruz along the north coast. TITSA line 363 runs along this coast from Puerto de la Cruz. There are free car parks on the seafront by the pools.
garachico.tips: The pools are conditions-dependent and are at their best roughly May to October; in heavy swell they are dangerous and closed, and that should be respected. The north is cooler and cloudier than the south, so bring a layer. Combine it with Icod de los Vinos and its dragon tree, fifteen minutes away.
faq: Can you swim in the rock pools at Garachico?
Yes, on calm days, and they are one of the most enjoyable swims in the north. They are closed and genuinely dangerous when the Atlantic swell is up, so check conditions and obey any closures.
Is Garachico worth visiting?
It is many visitors' favourite town on the island: compact, historic and beautiful, with the rock pools as a bonus. Half a day minimum, and better as an overnight stop.

drago-milenario.name: Drago Milenario
drago-milenario.alt: The Drago Milenario dragon tree at Icod de los Vinos
drago-milenario.tagline: The vast dragon tree of Icod, a symbol of the Canaries and probably around 800 years old.
drago-milenario.intro: The Drago Milenario stands at the edge of Icod de los Vinos, an enormous dragon tree whose name claims a thousand years. Botanists put it closer to eight hundred, which is still remarkable for a species that leaves no growth rings to count. It is the emblem of the archipelago and the reason most visitors stop in Icod at all.
drago-milenario.see: The tree is the sight. Paid entry to the Parque del Drago gets you close-up paths and a small botanical collection of Canarian species. Being honest, the free viewpoint beside the church square gives you a genuinely good view of the tree without the ticket, and many visitors are happy with that. The old town around Plaza de la Pila is pleasant for an hour, and Icod is a wine town, so a malvasía tasting fits naturally.
drago-milenario.getting: Roughly twenty minutes west of Puerto de la Cruz, or an hour and a half from the southern resorts. TITSA line 363 serves Icod along the north coast. There is paid parking near the park.
drago-milenario.tips: Decide in advance whether you want the ticket or the free view, as it changes how long you need from an hour to about fifteen minutes. Combine with Garachico, fifteen minutes further west, which most people find the more rewarding stop.
faq: Is the Drago Milenario really a thousand years old?
Probably not. The name means thousand-year dragon tree, but estimates put it closer to eight hundred years. Dragon trees produce no growth rings, so precise dating is impossible.
Do you have to pay to see the dragon tree?
No. Paid entry to Parque del Drago gets you closer and adds a small botanical garden, but there is a good free view from beside the church square.
drago-milenario.title: Drago Milenario, Icod — The Dragon Tree

playa-jardin.name: Playa Jardín
playa-jardin.alt: The seafront at Puerto de la Cruz
playa-jardin.tagline: Black volcanic sand backed by gardens designed by César Manrique, on the north coast.
playa-jardin.intro: Playa Jardín is the main beach of Puerto de la Cruz: three linked bays of black volcanic sand, landscaped behind with subtropical gardens laid out by the Lanzarote artist César Manrique. It is the north's answer to the resort beaches of the south, and it looks nothing like them.
playa-jardin.see: The gardens are as much of the attraction as the sand, full of palms and flowering shrubs with paths winding through. The beach faces the open Atlantic, so waves are part of the deal and surfers use it. Along the seafront you can walk to the old harbour and Plaza del Charco, and to the Lago Martiánez lido complex, also a Manrique design, which exists precisely because swimming in this sea is not always an option.
playa-jardin.getting: In Puerto de la Cruz, walkable from most of the town. From the southern resorts allow an hour and a quarter by car, or take the direct TITSA 343 bus, which runs a few times a day via both airports.
playa-jardin.tips: Watch the flags. This is a real Atlantic beach with genuine surf, and it behaves very differently from the sheltered southern bays. If the sea is rough, the Lago Martiánez lido nearby costs a few euros and solves the problem. The north is a few degrees cooler than the south with a real chance of morning cloud in any month.
faq: Can you swim at Playa Jardín?
Often yes, but this is an open Atlantic beach with real waves and currents. Follow the flags, and use the Lago Martiánez lido nearby when the sea is rough.
Why is the sand black at Playa Jardín?
It is the island's natural volcanic sand. The golden beaches of the south are mostly imported.

el-medano.name: El Médano
el-medano.alt: Kites over the beach at El Médano with Montaña Roja behind
el-medano.tagline: A low-rise surf town wrapped around a sandy bay, and one of Europe's best-known wind-sports spots.
el-medano.intro: El Médano is what the south of Tenerife looks like without the resorts: a real Canarian town on a wide sandy bay, ten minutes from the airport, where the constant trade winds have built one of Europe's great windsurfing and kitesurfing scenes. Board shops, surf cafés and a wooden boardwalk set the tone.
el-medano.see: The bay fills with sails on most summer days and the kite beach at El Cabezo, just east of town, is where the serious riders go. Schools run lessons year-round for beginners. The boardwalk links the plaza, the cafés and the beaches, and the red cone of Montaña Roja rises at the far end with an easy path to the summit and the best coastal view in the area. La Tejita, a long natural beach with a naturist section, sits just beyond it.
el-medano.getting: About ten minutes from Tenerife South Airport, which makes it the easiest arrival on the island. TITSA line 470 links it with Los Abrigos, Golf del Sur, Las Galletas and Los Cristianos. Town parking is tight on Wednesday and Saturday market mornings.
el-medano.tips: Be honest with yourself about wind. It is most reliable from May to September and peaks in July and August, which is superb for sport and genuinely annoying for lying on a towel. Autumn and early winter bring calmer days. Playa Chica is the sheltered corner when it blows.
faq: Is El Médano too windy for a beach holiday?
It can be. The trade winds are strongest from May to September. If you want still days on the sand, choose the south-west resorts or visit in autumn.
Can beginners learn to kitesurf in El Médano?
Yes. Several schools run lessons year-round, with tasters from around a hundred and twenty euros and longer beginner courses over several days.
el-medano.title: El Médano, Tenerife — Town, Beach & Wind Guide

montana-roja.name: Montaña Roja
montana-roja.alt: The Montaña Roja volcanic cone behind the beach
montana-roja.tagline: A 171-metre red volcanic cone between two beaches, with the best coastal panorama in the south-east.
montana-roja.intro: Montaña Roja is the red cone that anchors the coast between El Médano and La Tejita. It is protected as a special nature reserve for its dune habitat and birdlife, and a short, steep path climbs to the summit for a view along the whole south-eastern shoreline.
montana-roja.see: The climb is the thing: roughly thirty to forty minutes up over loose stones, with the reward of the coast laid out below and the kites of El Médano on one side, the long sweep of La Tejita on the other. Easier paths cross the reserve at the base and link the two beaches, which makes a pleasant circular walk of about two hours if you take in both.
montana-roja.getting: Two free dirt car parks off the TF-643 between El Médano and Los Abrigos serve both the trailhead and La Tejita, with a five-minute walk over the dunes. From El Médano you can walk out along the coast instead.
montana-roja.tips: There is no shade anywhere on the climb, so go early or late and take water. The stones are loose on the descent, so proper shoes help. Summer weekends fill the car parks. Combine it with a swim at La Tejita, remembering that the eastern end of that beach is a long-established naturist area.
highlights: Best coastal view in the south-east
Links El Médano and La Tejita
faq: How hard is the Montaña Roja climb?
It is short but steep, roughly thirty to forty minutes up on loose stones. Most reasonably fit walkers manage it, but there is no shade at all.
Is La Tejita a nudist beach?
Partly. The eastern end nearest Montaña Roja is a long-established naturist area, while the rest of the beach is mixed.
montana-roja.title: Montaña Roja, Tenerife — Walk & Viewpoint

la-laguna.name: San Cristóbal de La Laguna
la-laguna.alt: A colonial street in La Laguna's old town
la-laguna.tagline: Tenerife's original capital, a UNESCO World Heritage grid whose plan was copied across colonial Latin America.
la-laguna.intro: La Laguna was the island's first capital and is now a lively university town, listed by UNESCO since 1999 because its unfortified sixteenth-century grid became the model for Spanish colonial cities in the Americas. The old centre is pastel mansions, carved wooden balconies and pedestrian streets full of students, and it has the best-value tapas on the island.
la-laguna.see: Wander first: Calle Obispo Rey Redondo and Calle Herradores are the spine, lined with cafés and tapas bars. Climb the tower of the Iglesia de la Concepción for a couple of euros and the best view over the grid of roofs. Plaza del Adelantado anchors the old town, and the cathedral and the historic mansions fill the streets between. In the evening the tapas bars are the point.
la-laguna.getting: Tram line 1 links Santa Cruz with La Laguna in about thirty to forty minutes for well under two euros, which is by far the easiest way. From the southern resorts, take the 110 or 111 express bus to Santa Cruz and change to the tram, or drive in about an hour.
la-laguna.tips: At around 550 metres the town is several degrees cooler than the coast, and locals call it the fridge of Tenerife, so bring a layer even in summer. The old town is pedestrianised, so park on the edge. Pair it with Anaga, which begins just above the town.
faq: Why is La Laguna a UNESCO site?
Its unfortified grid plan from the late fifteenth and sixteenth centuries became the template for Spanish colonial towns across the Americas, and the historic centre survives largely intact.
How do you get to La Laguna from Santa Cruz?
Tram line 1 runs between the two in roughly thirty to forty minutes for a couple of euros, and it is much easier than driving and parking.
la-laguna.title: La Laguna, Tenerife — UNESCO Old Town Guide

cruz-del-carmen.name: Cruz del Carmen
cruz-del-carmen.tagline: The gateway to the Anaga laurel forest, with a visitor centre, a mirador and the easiest trails into the woods.
cruz-del-carmen.intro: Cruz del Carmen sits on the Anaga ridge above La Laguna and is where most people start exploring the range. There is a visitor centre, a viewpoint over the valley and, crucially, the trailheads into the laurisilva, an ancient laurel forest that has survived here since before the last ice age.
cruz-del-carmen.see: The Sendero de los Sentidos, the path of the senses, is a set of short, easy loops from the car park that take between half an hour and just over an hour and give you the forest without a serious hike. Longer routes run from here down towards Punta del Hidalgo or across to Taganana, taking three to five hours. The mirador beside the centre looks back over the La Laguna plain when the cloud allows.
cruz-del-carmen.getting: About thirty minutes from La Laguna or Santa Cruz on the TF-12, a winding but manageable mountain road. There is a car park at the visitor centre which fills at weekends, so arrive early. Buses into Anaga are sparse, so a car or a guided tour is realistic.
cruz-del-carmen.tips: Expect mist and drizzle on the ridge even when the coast is in full sun. That cloud is exactly what feeds the forest, so treat it as part of the experience and bring a layer and grippy shoes. Note that some protected routes, such as the Bosque Encantado at El Pijaral, require a free permit booked in advance.
highlights: Easy Sendero de los Sentidos loops
faq: Do you need a permit to hike in Anaga?
Not for most trails, including the Sendero de los Sentidos. Some protected routes such as the Bosque Encantado at El Pijaral do require a free permit booked in advance.
Is Anaga always misty?
Often, on the ridge. Trade-wind cloud sits against these mountains and is what keeps the laurel forest alive, so plan for it rather than against it.
cruz-del-carmen.title: Cruz del Carmen, Anaga — Trails & Visitor Centre

playa-de-la-arena.name: Playa de la Arena
playa-de-la-arena.alt: The black sand and promenade at Playa de la Arena
playa-de-la-arena.tagline: A compact beach of jet-black volcanic sand that has flown the Blue Flag for over twenty-five years.
playa-de-la-arena.intro: Playa de la Arena is the main beach of the western resort strip, a small, tidy bay of genuinely black volcanic sand beneath the shoulder of the Los Gigantes cliffs. It is well serviced, easy to reach and popular, and it is the best swimming beach on this coast when conditions allow.
playa-de-la-arena.see: The beach is compact, so it can feel busy in high season, but the facilities are good: loungers, showers and lifeguards, with bars and restaurants directly behind. The coastal walkway links it with Puerto de Santiago and on towards Los Gigantes marina, which makes an easy stroll and a good way to reach the boat trips.
playa-de-la-arena.getting: Roughly twenty-five to thirty-five minutes from Costa Adeje via the TF-1 and TF-47, and about forty-five minutes from Tenerife South Airport.
playa-de-la-arena.tips: Respect the red flags. The swell on this coast is real and the beach is closed to swimming more often than the sheltered southern bays. Black sand gets genuinely hot underfoot in the middle of the day, so bring something for your feet. The whole coast faces west, so stay for the sunset.
faq: Is Playa de la Arena safe for swimming?
On calm days yes, and it is the best swimming beach on this stretch. The Atlantic swell here is real, though, so always follow the flags.
Why is the sand black at Playa de la Arena?
It is natural volcanic sand, which is what most of the island's beaches look like away from the imported golden sand of the south.

mount-teide.name: Mount Teide
mount-teide.alt: The peak of Mount Teide above the crater floor
mount-teide.title: Mount Teide, Tenerife — Cable Car, Summit & Tips
mount-teide.tagline: Spain's highest peak at 3,715 metres, and the reason the island looks the way it does.
mount-teide.intro: Teide rises 3,715 metres out of the Atlantic, which makes it the highest point in Spain and, measured from the ocean floor, one of the tallest volcanic structures on Earth. The national park around it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007 and is among the most visited national parks anywhere. Even if you never leave the coast, the mountain is on your horizon most days.
mount-teide.see: Most visitors take the cable car from the base station up to around 3,555 metres, an eight-minute ride that leaves a short walk to two viewpoints. Going higher, onto the Telesforo Bravo path to the actual crater rim, needs a free permit booked in advance through the national parks website, and the daily quota goes early. Lower down, the crater floor is arguably the better experience: the Roques de García rock formations, the Llano de Ucanca plain and a landscape so lunar that film crews use it. After dark the park is one of the world's better stargazing sites, with organised night tours from the resorts.
mount-teide.getting: About an hour and a half by car from the southern resorts on the TF-21 via Vilaflor, or from the north via La Orotava. Two TITSA buses serve the park daily: the 342 from Costa Adeje and the 348 from Puerto de la Cruz, both leaving in the morning and returning mid-afternoon. Many visitors book a guided tour instead, which removes the mountain driving and usually includes the cable car.
mount-teide.tips: It is genuinely cold up there. The summit can sit below freezing while the coast is in shorts weather, and the wind makes it worse, so bring layers whatever the forecast says at sea level. The cable car closes in high wind, which happens often enough to be worth checking before you drive up. Altitude affects some people at 3,555 metres; take it slowly, and anyone with heart or breathing problems should think carefully. Book the summit permit and the cable car well ahead in peak season.
highlights: Roques de García and the crater floor
faq: Do you need a permit to climb Mount Teide?

You need a free permit only for the Telesforo Bravo path above the cable car station to the actual summit. It is booked in advance through the national parks reservation website and the daily quota fills early. Everything below that, including the cable car and the crater floor, is open to all.
How cold is it at the top of Teide?
Much colder than the coast — often near or below freezing at the top station, and windier. Take proper layers even on a hot day at sea level.
Can you get to Teide by bus?

Yes. TITSA line 342 runs from Costa Adeje and 348 from Puerto de la Cruz, once each per day, up in the morning and back in the afternoon. It works, but it gives you a fixed and fairly short window in the park.

loro-parque.name: Loro Parque
loro-parque.title: Loro Parque, Tenerife — Visitor Guide & Tickets
loro-parque.tagline: The north's biggest attraction: a zoo and botanical park that began as a parrot collection in 1972.
loro-parque.intro: Loro Parque opened in Puerto de la Cruz in 1972 with a few dozen parrots and has grown into the north's flagship attraction, part zoo and part botanical garden, set in dense subtropical planting. The parrot collection remains one of the largest in the world and is what the name still refers to.
loro-parque.see: Beyond the parrots there are penguins in a refrigerated hall, gorillas, big cats, an aquarium with a shark tunnel, and animal presentations through the day. The planting is a genuine attraction in itself. Allow the best part of a day. Worth knowing before you book: like other parks that keep marine mammals, Loro Parque draws criticism from animal welfare campaigners, and its cetacean collection has changed in recent years — check the park's own site for what is currently on show rather than relying on older guides.
loro-parque.getting: In Puerto de la Cruz, with a free vintage-style train shuttling from the town centre. From the southern resorts allow an hour and a quarter by car, or take the direct TITSA 343 bus. Twin tickets combining Loro Parque with Siam Park in the south are sold at both parks and by tour operators, and work out cheaper than two separate day tickets.
loro-parque.tips: Go early, both for the animals and for the queues. The north is cooler and cloudier than the south, so a jacket is sensible even in summer, and the penguin house is deliberately cold. If you are staying in the south, the twin ticket only pays off if you will genuinely use both parks, since they are an hour and a half apart.
highlights: One of the world's largest parrot collections
faq: Is Loro Parque worth visiting?

For most visitors to the north, yes — it is the biggest attraction on that coast and the botanical setting is genuinely good. Visitors uncomfortable with marine mammals in captivity should check the park's current animal collection before booking.
Is the twin ticket with Siam Park worth it?
Only if you will use both. The two parks are an hour and a half apart on opposite coasts, so it means two separate day trips, but the combined price is well below two single tickets.

puerto-de-la-cruz.name: Puerto de la Cruz
puerto-de-la-cruz.alt: The Lago Martiánez lido at Puerto de la Cruz
puerto-de-la-cruz.title: Puerto de la Cruz, Tenerife — Town Guide
puerto-de-la-cruz.tagline: Tenerife's original resort town, and still the one that feels most like a real Canarian place.
puerto-de-la-cruz.intro: Puerto de la Cruz was welcoming visitors long before the southern resorts existed, and it wears that history well. It is a proper town rather than a strip: a working plaza, an old harbour, steep streets of Canarian houses, and a seafront built around the fact that the Atlantic here is often too rough to swim in.
puerto-de-la-cruz.see: Lago Martiánez, the seawater lido complex designed by César Manrique, is the town's clever answer to that rough sea and a fine place to spend an afternoon. Playa Jardín, also landscaped by Manrique, is the main black-sand beach. Plaza del Charco is the social centre, ringed by cafés under old laurel trees, and the lanes around the old harbour repay an aimless wander. Loro Parque is a short shuttle ride away, and the botanical garden on the edge of town is one of the oldest in Spain.
puerto-de-la-cruz.getting: An hour and a quarter from the southern resorts by car on the TF-1 and TF-5, or on the direct TITSA 343 bus, which calls at both airports. From Santa Cruz it is around forty minutes. The town centre is walkable and parking is easier in the underground car parks than on the street.
puerto-de-la-cruz.tips: This is the north, and the north has weather. Mornings can be cloudy when the south is clear, and it is a few degrees cooler year-round — pack a layer even in August. That trade-off buys you greenery, better food and lower prices than Costa Adeje. Carnival here in February is a serious event and accommodation books out well ahead.
highlights: Plaza del Charco and the old town
faq: Is Puerto de la Cruz better than the south?
Different rather than better. It has more character, better food and lower prices, but cooler and cloudier weather and rougher sea. Sun-certainty favours the south; atmosphere favours the north.
Can you swim in Puerto de la Cruz?
Sometimes. Playa Jardín is an open Atlantic beach where the flags matter. The Lago Martiánez lido exists precisely for the days when the sea is rough.

los-cristianos.name: Los Cristianos
los-cristianos.alt: The bay and town of Los Cristianos
los-cristianos.title: Los Cristianos, Tenerife — Resort & Town Guide
los-cristianos.tagline: A former fishing village that grew into a resort without losing its town centre, and the island's ferry port for La Gomera.
los-cristianos.intro: Los Cristianos sits at the southern end of the resort strip and is the most lived-in of them. There is still an old town behind the harbour, a Sunday market, and streets where the businesses serve residents rather than visitors. It is flatter and more walkable than its neighbours, which is one reason it is popular with older travellers and with visitors who have mobility needs.
los-cristianos.see: Two beaches: Playa de los Cristianos by the harbour, and the far bigger Playa de las Vistas along the promenade. The working port is the departure point for ferries to La Gomera, La Palma and El Hierro, which makes a day trip to La Gomera genuinely easy. Whale-watching boats leave from the same harbour. The promenade runs unbroken to Playa de las Américas and on to Costa Adeje, so evenings tend to involve a long flat walk and dinner somewhere along it.
los-cristianos.getting: Fifteen to twenty minutes from Tenerife South Airport on the TF-1. It is the main southern hub for TITSA buses, including the 111 and 110 express services to Santa Cruz, so it is the easiest southern base if you are not hiring a car.
los-cristianos.tips: For eating, walk a street or two back from the seafront where the prices drop and the cooking improves. The Sunday morning market near the harbour is worth timing your week around. If you want nightlife, this is the quiet end — Playa de las Américas is a twenty-minute walk north.
highlights: Ferries to La Gomera and La Palma
faq: Is Los Cristianos good for older visitors?
It is one of the best choices on the island. The seafront is flat and continuous, the beaches have assisted bathing services, and the town has a real centre rather than only bars and tourist shops.
Can you get to La Gomera from Los Cristianos?
Yes. Ferries run from the harbour several times a day and the crossing takes under an hour, which makes a day trip realistic.

costa-adeje.name: Costa Adeje
costa-adeje.alt: Thatched parasols and sunbeds on a Costa Adeje beach
costa-adeje.title: Costa Adeje, Tenerife — Resort Area Guide
costa-adeje.tagline: The upmarket end of the southern coast: the best hotels, the smartest beaches and the highest prices.
costa-adeje.intro: Costa Adeje is the purpose-built resort that runs north from Playa de las Américas to the old village of La Caleta. It holds most of the island's five-star hotels, a string of well-kept Blue Flag beaches and a promenade that ties it all together. It is comfortable rather than characterful, and it makes no apology for that.
costa-adeje.see: The beaches step up in polish as you go north: Torviscas, then Fañabé, then Playa del Duque at the smart end. Siam Park sits above the resort and is the strongest single attraction in the south. Whale-watching boats leave from Puerto Colón marina. La Caleta at the northern edge has the best fish restaurants on this coast, and Plaza del Duque is the island's most upmarket shopping centre.
costa-adeje.getting: Twenty to twenty-five minutes from Tenerife South Airport on the TF-1. Taxis and pre-booked transfers are straightforward; the TITSA 111 also runs from the airport. Within the resort almost everything is walkable along the seafront.
costa-adeje.tips: Prices here are the island's highest, and the gap is real — the same dinner costs noticeably less in Los Cristianos twenty minutes south. The trade-off is quieter, better-maintained beaches and stronger hotels. For nightlife you will be heading to Las Américas; Costa Adeje goes quiet early, which for most visitors is the point.
highlights: Most of the island's five-star hotels
Blue Flag beaches in a row
faq: Is Costa Adeje better than Playa de las Américas?

For families, couples and anyone wanting quiet, yes — the beaches and hotels are better kept. Las Américas is cheaper and far livelier at night. They are a twenty-minute walk apart, so you can use both.
Is Costa Adeje expensive?
It is the most expensive part of the island for hotels and restaurants. Eating a street back from the seafront, or driving to Los Cristianos, cuts the bill significantly.

playa-de-las-americas.name: Playa de las Américas
playa-de-las-americas.alt: Palms along the promenade at Playa de las Américas
playa-de-las-americas.title: Playa de las Américas — Resort & Nightlife Guide
playa-de-las-americas.tagline: The island's nightlife capital, cheaper than its neighbours and unapologetic about what it is.
playa-de-las-americas.intro: Playa de las Américas is the busiest and loudest of the southern resorts, built in the 1970s and 80s with no pretence of being a Canarian town. What it offers is a run of decent beaches, a huge choice of cheap places to eat and drink, and the island's only real concentration of nightlife.
playa-de-las-americas.see: Playa de Troya and Playa del Camisón are the main beaches, the latter smaller, more sheltered and generally the nicer of the two. The promenade connects everything and runs both north into Costa Adeje and south into Los Cristianos. The nightlife clusters around the Veronicas strip, which is exactly as advertised and easily avoided if it is not your thing — a few hundred metres away the resort is unremarkably quiet.
playa-de-las-americas.getting: Around fifteen to twenty minutes from Tenerife South Airport on the TF-1, with the same taxi, transfer and TITSA options as the other southern resorts. Everything within the resort is walkable.
playa-de-las-americas.tips: Choose your street carefully. Hotels within earshot of the Veronicas strip are cheap for a reason, and the difference between a noisy block and a quiet one can be two hundred metres. Playa del Camisón is the beach to pick with children. If you want value without the volume, look at Los Cristianos instead.
highlights: Playa del Camisón and Playa de Troya
faq: Is Playa de las Américas suitable for families?
Parts of it are. The beaches are good and Playa del Camisón in particular suits children. Choose a hotel well away from the Veronicas nightlife strip and check reviews for noise.
Is Playa de las Américas cheaper than Costa Adeje?
Yes, noticeably, for both hotels and eating out. The beaches and hotel standards are a step below, and it is much livelier at night.

santa-cruz.name: Santa Cruz de Tenerife
santa-cruz.alt: The Auditorio de Tenerife on the Santa Cruz waterfront
santa-cruz.title: Santa Cruz de Tenerife — City Guide
santa-cruz.tagline: The island's capital: a working Spanish city with a Calatrava landmark, a famous market and the world's second-largest carnival.
santa-cruz.intro: Santa Cruz is where the island actually works. It is a port city rather than a resort, with department stores, office workers and a waterfront that has been rebuilt around Santiago Calatrava's Auditorio. Visitors who only see the south often skip it, which is a mistake if you want any sense of what Tenerife is like when it is not selling itself.
santa-cruz.see: The Auditorio is the landmark, its great white wave visible from the motorway. Plaza de España is built around a shallow artificial lake designed by Herzog & de Meuron. The Mercado de Nuestra Señora de África is the best market on the island for produce, cheese and fish. Add the TEA arts centre, the palm-filled Parque García Sanabria and Calle del Castillo for shopping. In February the city hosts a carnival that is generally reckoned second only to Rio.
santa-cruz.getting: About an hour from the southern resorts on the TF-1, and much easier by the TITSA 110 or 111 express coaches, which run frequently and drop you at the intercambiador in the centre. From there tram line 1 continues to La Laguna. Driving in is fine; parking is easiest in the underground car parks near the Auditorio.
santa-cruz.tips: Most shops still close for a long lunch and stay shut on Sunday, so plan around that. The market is a morning place. Combine the city with La Laguna, thirty minutes away by tram, and you have a full and genuinely interesting day. If you are here in February, book accommodation months ahead.
highlights: Mercado de Nuestra Señora de África
faq: Is Santa Cruz worth a day trip?
Yes, particularly combined with La Laguna up the tram line. It is a real city rather than a resort, with the island's best market and shopping and a genuinely striking waterfront.
How do you get to Santa Cruz from the south?
The TITSA 110 and 111 express coaches run frequently from Los Cristianos and Costa Adeje and take around an hour, which is easier than driving and parking.

la-tejita.name: Playa de la Tejita
la-tejita.alt: Playa de la Tejita with Montaña Roja behind
la-tejita.title: Playa de la Tejita, Tenerife — Beach Guide
la-tejita.tagline: One of the longest natural beaches on the island, undeveloped, with Montaña Roja at one end.
la-tejita.intro: La Tejita runs for roughly a kilometre of natural golden sand between Montaña Roja and El Médano, and it is one of the few big beaches in the south with almost nothing built on it. That emptiness is the appeal, and it comes with the trade-offs you would expect: little shade, few facilities and an exposed Atlantic shoreline.
la-tejita.see: The beach and the volcano behind it are the whole attraction. The path up Montaña Roja starts at the eastern end and gives the best coastal view in this corner of the island. There is a beach bar at the western end in season. The eastern end, nearest the volcano, is a long-established naturist area; the rest is mixed and nobody makes a fuss either way.
la-tejita.getting: Two free dirt car parks off the TF-643 between El Médano and Los Abrigos put you five minutes from the sand across the dunes. It is around ten minutes from Tenerife South Airport, or a walk of about half an hour along the coast from El Médano.
la-tejita.tips: There is no natural shade, so bring an umbrella if you plan to stay. The same trade winds that make El Médano a windsurfing centre blow here, strongest between May and September — superb if you like a wild beach, wearing if you want to read a book. Swim with care: this is open Atlantic with no lifeguard cover along most of its length.
highlights: Around a kilometre of natural sand
Montaña Roja at the eastern end
Naturist section at the volcano end
faq: Is La Tejita a nudist beach?
Partly. The eastern end nearest Montaña Roja is a long-established naturist area. The rest of the beach is mixed and textile.
Is La Tejita windy?
Often, yes. It sits on the same stretch of coast as El Médano, where the trade winds are strongest from May to September. Autumn and early winter are calmer.

candelaria.name: Candelaria
candelaria.alt: The Basílica de Nuestra Señora de la Candelaria
candelaria.title: Candelaria, Tenerife — Basilica & Town Guide
candelaria.tagline: The spiritual capital of the Canary Islands, with nine bronze Guanche kings facing the sea.
candelaria.intro: Candelaria, on the east coast south of Santa Cruz, is where Canarians come rather than where tour buses stop. Its basilica holds the image of the Virgin of Candelaria, patron saint of the whole archipelago, and the square in front of it is guarded by nine bronze statues of Guanche kings looking out at the Atlantic.
candelaria.see: The Basílica de Nuestra Señora de la Candelaria dominates the seafront square, and the statues of the nine menceyes — the chiefs who ruled the island before the Spanish conquest — are the photograph everyone takes. Beyond that it is a pleasant coastal town with black-sand beaches, a promenade and unpretentious fish restaurants. The big pilgrimage falls in mid-August and draws people on foot from across the island.
candelaria.getting: Around twenty minutes south of Santa Cruz on the TF-1, or roughly forty-five minutes from the southern resorts. TITSA buses run along this coast from Santa Cruz. There is parking near the seafront, which fills on Sundays and during festivals.
candelaria.tips: Sunday is when the town is at its most alive and its most crowded. The beaches here are black volcanic sand and the sea is more exposed than the sheltered southern bays, so treat swimming with the usual Atlantic caution. It pairs well with the Güímar pyramids, twenty minutes further south.
highlights: Patron saint of the Canary Islands
faq: Who are the statues at Candelaria?
They are the nine menceyes, the Guanche chiefs who ruled the districts of Tenerife before the Spanish conquest. The bronzes stand along the seafront in front of the basilica.
Is Candelaria worth visiting?
If you want a side of the island that is not built for tourism, yes. It is the religious heart of the Canaries and a genuine Canarian town, best combined with the Güímar pyramids nearby.

punta-de-teno.name: Punta de Teno
punta-de-teno.alt: The red and white lighthouse at Punta de Teno
punta-de-teno.title: Punta de Teno, Tenerife — Lighthouse & Access
punta-de-teno.tagline: The island's western tip: a lighthouse, an empty headland and the finest view of the Los Gigantes cliffs.
punta-de-teno.intro: Punta de Teno is the westernmost point of Tenerife, a low volcanic headland with a red-and-white lighthouse at the end of it. There is nothing there but rock, sea and the view — south along the full wall of the Los Gigantes cliffs and out to La Gomera and La Palma on a clear day. Getting there is deliberately restricted, which is why it stays as good as it is.
punta-de-teno.see: The lighthouse and the headland around it, and the view. There is a small rocky cove for a swim on calm days, and the drive or ride in along the Teno cliffs is spectacular in its own right. Most visitors stay an hour. Sunset here is exceptional and is the reason the last shuttle back matters.
punta-de-teno.getting: Private cars are barred from the access road during the main part of the day, so nearly everyone arrives on the TITSA shuttle bus from Buenavista del Norte, a short and cheap ride. Check current times and any restrictions before you set off: the road runs beneath unstable cliffs and has closed for long spells after rockfalls, and the rules change accordingly.
punta-de-teno.tips: Take water and a hat — there is no shade and no café at the point. The wind here is stronger than the temperature suggests. Confirm the shuttle timetable and the road's status on the day rather than relying on an older guide, since this is the single most changeable access arrangement on the island.
highlights: Best view of the Los Gigantes cliffs
Reached by shuttle bus, not car
La Gomera and La Palma on the horizon
faq: Can you drive to Punta de Teno?
Generally not during the day. Private vehicles are restricted and visitors use the TITSA shuttle from Buenavista del Norte. Always check the current rules, as the access road closes after rockfalls.
Is Punta de Teno worth the trip?
For the view along the Los Gigantes cliffs, yes. It is an hour at the point plus a spectacular ride in, and it is one of the emptiest places on an otherwise busy island.

playa-de-fanabe.name: Playa de Fañabé
playa-de-fanabe.alt: Playa de Fañabé seen from the promenade above
playa-de-fanabe.tagline: The big, busy family beach at the heart of Costa Adeje, with everything laid on behind it.
playa-de-fanabe.intro: Playa de Fañabé is the long golden beach in the middle of Costa Adeje, and the one most package holidays end up walking down to. It is Blue Flag, well serviced and backed by a solid wall of hotels, which tells you both what is good about it and what is not: everything you need is thirty seconds away, and you will not have it to yourself.
playa-de-fanabe.see: Swimming, sunbathing and watersports, mostly. The sand is imported and golden, the water is usually calm enough for children, and there are lifeguards in season. Parasailing, jet skis and banana boats operate off the beach through the summer. The promenade behind runs north to Playa del Duque and south towards Playa de las Américas, and Puerto Colón marina, five minutes away, is where the whale-watching and catamaran trips leave from.
playa-de-fanabe.getting: About twenty to twenty-five minutes from Tenerife South Airport on the TF-1, and a flat walk from most of Costa Adeje. TITSA buses serve the resort from Los Cristianos and Playa de las Américas. Street parking near the beach is scarce in high season; the hotel car parks are the realistic option.
playa-de-fanabe.tips: The middle of the beach is the busiest part, and it thins out noticeably at either end. Sunbeds cost a little less here than at Playa del Duque next door. Prices at the seafront restaurants reflect their position, so walk one street back if you are eating more than once. Afternoon breeze picks up along this whole coast, which is welcome on the sand and less so if you are trying to read.
highlights: Promenade to Duque and Las Américas
faq: Is Playa de Fañabé good for families?
Yes. The water is usually calm, there are lifeguards in season, and the facilities behind the beach are excellent. It is busier than Playa del Duque and cheaper for sunbeds.
Is the sand at Fañabé natural?
No. Like most of the golden beaches in the south, the sand was brought in. The island's natural sand is the black volcanic kind you see in the north and west.

playa-del-camison.name: Playa del Camisón
playa-del-camison.alt: Thatched parasols on Playa del Camisón
playa-del-camison.tagline: The nicest beach in Playa de las Américas: small, sheltered and a clear step above its neighbours.
playa-del-camison.intro: Playa del Camisón is a compact crescent of golden sand at the quieter end of Playa de las Américas, tucked behind breakwaters that keep the water flat. It is smaller than Playa de Troya up the coast and considerably more pleasant, which is why regulars to this resort tend to walk past two other beaches to get to it.
playa-del-camison.see: It is a beach for swimming and sitting rather than doing. The sheltered water suits children and weaker swimmers, there are showers, sunbeds and lifeguards in season, and the palm-lined promenade runs directly behind. From here you can walk south into Los Cristianos in about twenty minutes or north through Las Américas towards Costa Adeje.
playa-del-camison.getting: Fifteen to twenty minutes from Tenerife South Airport on the TF-1, at the southern end of Playa de las Américas near the Mare Nostrum complex. It is walkable from anywhere in the resort and from Los Cristianos along the seafront.
playa-del-camison.tips: Because it is small it fills early, so mornings are better in high season. It is a good choice if you are staying in Las Américas with children but want to avoid the busier central beaches. The promenade here is one of the better evening walks on this coast, and it is flat the whole way.
faq: Which is the best beach in Playa de las Américas?
Playa del Camisón is generally reckoned the nicest: it is smaller, more sheltered and quieter than Playa de Troya. It is at the Los Cristianos end of the resort.
Is Playa del Camisón good for children?
Yes. Breakwaters keep the water calm, the sand shelves gently and there are lifeguards in season.

los-abrigos.name: Los Abrigos
los-abrigos.alt: A palm-lined street in Los Abrigos
los-abrigos.tagline: A working fishing village ten minutes from the airport, and the south's best-value place to eat fish.
los-abrigos.intro: Los Abrigos is a small, low-rise village on the south-east coast that has done very well out of one thing: fish. A row of restaurants along the seafront serves what the boats bring in, and Canarians drive down from across the island to eat there. It is not a beach destination and makes no attempt to be one.
los-abrigos.see: Eating is the reason to come. The seafront restaurants are unpretentious and the fish is priced by weight, which is normal here and worth knowing before you order. Beyond that there is a small harbour, a set of natural rock pools along the coast to the east, and a walkable stretch of shoreline. Most visits last an evening.
los-abrigos.getting: About ten minutes from Tenerife South Airport, which makes it a genuinely good first or last meal of a trip. Roughly twenty minutes from Los Cristianos on the TF-1, and TITSA line 470 links it with El Médano, Golf del Sur and Los Cristianos. Parking on the seafront is tight at dinner.
los-abrigos.tips: Book at weekends, when locals fill the tables. Fish is sold by weight, so ask the price per kilo and roughly what your fish weighs before agreeing — nobody minds the question. There is no sandy beach here; La Tejita and El Médano are ten minutes away if you want one. The village is exposed to the same trade winds as that coast.
faq: Why is Los Abrigos known for fish?
It is a working fishing village, and its seafront restaurants sell the local catch simply cooked and priced by weight. It has a strong reputation among Canarians, not just visitors.
Is Los Abrigos worth visiting?
For a meal, yes, especially on your first or last night given it is ten minutes from the airport. There is no beach, so it is an evening rather than a day.

piramides-de-guimar.name: Pirámides de Güímar
piramides-de-guimar.alt: A stepped pyramid at the Pirámides de Güímar park
piramides-de-guimar.title: Pirámides de Güímar — Visitor Guide & The Debate
piramides-de-guimar.tagline: Six stepped platforms of lava stone, a Norwegian explorer, and an argument that is still going.
piramides-de-guimar.intro: On the edge of Güímar stand six rectangular stepped structures built from lava stone. Thor Heyerdahl, the Norwegian who sailed the Kon-Tiki, moved to Tenerife in the 1990s, became convinced they were ancient, and set up the ethnographic park that protects them today. Mainstream archaeology is far less convinced, and that unresolved argument is much of what makes the visit interesting.
piramides-de-guimar.see: The pyramids themselves, plus a well-made museum covering Heyerdahl's expeditions, a replica of the Ra II reed boat, and gardens planted with species from the places his voyages touched. The park sets out the competing explanations fairly: Heyerdahl's transatlantic theory on one hand, and the widely held view that the structures are nineteenth-century terracing built from stones cleared off farmland on the other. Allow around two hours.
piramides-de-guimar.getting: Roughly thirty minutes south of Santa Cruz on the TF-1, or about forty-five minutes from the southern resorts. There is parking at the park. Buses run to Güímar from Santa Cruz, with a short walk or taxi at the far end.
piramides-de-guimar.tips: Go for the ideas as much as the stones — visitors expecting Egypt are usually disappointed, while visitors who enjoy an unresolved argument tend to leave happy. Much of the site is outdoors with limited shade. It combines neatly with Candelaria, twenty minutes north up the coast.
highlights: Thor Heyerdahl's museum and Ra II replica
faq: Are the Güímar pyramids really ancient?

That is disputed. Thor Heyerdahl argued they were, and built a case around transatlantic contact. The prevailing archaeological view is that they are nineteenth-century agricultural terracing made from field stones. The park presents both.
Is it worth visiting the Pirámides de Güímar?
If you enjoy the argument and the Heyerdahl story, yes — the museum is good and it takes about two hours. Visitors expecting monumental ancient architecture usually find it underwhelming.

taganana.name: Taganana
taganana.alt: The village of Taganana in a valley of the Anaga mountains above the Atlantic
taganana.tagline: One of the oldest settlements on the island, spilled down an Anaga valley towards the sea.
taganana.intro: Taganana sits in a steep green valley on the north side of the Anaga massif, white houses scattered among terraces of vines. It was settled very soon after the Spanish conquest and stayed effectively cut off for centuries — the road over the ridge is recent history. It remains one of the most striking approaches on the island.
taganana.see: The village itself is a short wander: the church of Nuestra Señora de las Nieves, narrow lanes and terraced vineyards that still produce wine. What most people really come for is the coast just below — Roque de las Bodegas with its fish restaurants, then Almáciga, then Benijo at the end of the road. Walking trails climb from the village back up into the laurel forest.
taganana.getting: About forty-five minutes from Santa Cruz over the Anaga ridge on the TF-12 and TF-134, a beautiful and continuously winding drive through the laurel forest. Buses into Anaga are infrequent, so most visitors drive or take a guided tour. Parking in the village is very limited.
taganana.tips: Expect cloud on the ridge on the way over even when the coast below is clear — that is how Anaga works. Combine the village with lunch at Roque de las Bodegas and the drive on to Benijo, which is the natural half-day. Anyone prone to car sickness should take the front seat and allow far longer than the distance suggests.
highlights: Fish restaurants at Roque de las Bodegas
faq: How do you get to Taganana?
By car over the Anaga ridge from Santa Cruz or La Laguna, around forty-five minutes on very winding mountain roads. Public transport into Anaga is sparse, so most visitors drive or join a tour.
Is there a beach at Taganana?
Not in the village itself, but the coast road below leads to Roque de las Bodegas, Almáciga and Benijo. These are wild Atlantic beaches with strong currents, better for looking than swimming.

punta-del-hidalgo.name: Punta del Hidalgo
punta-del-hidalgo.alt: Punta del Hidalgo and the Atlantic seen from the hills above
punta-del-hidalgo.tagline: Natural seawater pools at the end of the north coast road, where Anaga meets the Atlantic.
punta-del-hidalgo.intro: Punta del Hidalgo is where the road along the north coast from La Laguna runs out, at the foot of the Anaga mountains. It is a village of locals rather than visitors, and its draw is a set of natural and part-built seawater pools along a rocky shore, plus some of the best walking on this side of the island starting from the edge of town.
punta-del-hidalgo.see: The rock pools are the main event and are free to use, sheltered enough to swim in on calm days. A strikingly modern concrete lighthouse stands at the point. The coastal path west to Bajamar is an easy walk of about an hour, and steeper trails climb from here up into Anaga towards Chinamada and its cave houses. There are unfussy local restaurants along the front.
punta-del-hidalgo.getting: Around twenty-five minutes from La Laguna on the TF-13, or forty minutes from Santa Cruz. TITSA buses run from La Laguna. From the southern resorts, allow an hour and a quarter, or take the express coach to Santa Cruz and continue by tram and bus.
punta-del-hidalgo.tips: The pools depend entirely on the sea state. In swell they are dangerous and should be left alone; on a calm day they are excellent. This coast is cooler and cloudier than the south, so bring a layer. Sunday is when the village is at its most Canarian and its busiest.
faq: Can you swim at Punta del Hidalgo?
In the seawater pools, yes, on calm days — they are free and popular with locals. When the Atlantic swell is up they become dangerous and should be avoided.
Is Punta del Hidalgo worth visiting?
If you want the north coast without tourism, yes. It is a real village with free sea pools and excellent walking, and it pairs well with Bajamar or a hike into Anaga.

la-orotava.name: La Orotava
la-orotava.alt: The carved wooden balconies of the Casa de los Balcones in La Orotava
la-orotava.title: La Orotava, Tenerife — Historic Town Guide
la-orotava.tagline: Steep cobbled streets and carved Canarian balconies, on the hillside above Puerto de la Cruz.
la-orotava.intro: La Orotava sits above Puerto de la Cruz on the slope running down from Teide, and it is the best-preserved historic town in the north. Wealth from sugar and wine built it, and the money shows: carved wooden balconies, painted mansions and a hillside grid of cobbled streets steep enough to make you notice.
la-orotava.see: The Casa de los Balcones is the landmark, a seventeenth-century house whose galleried Canarian pine balconies appear on half the postcards of the island. The Iglesia de la Concepción has one of the finest baroque façades in the Canaries, and the Victoria Gardens step up the hillside behind. At Corpus Christi the town lays enormous carpets of coloured volcanic sand across the square in front of the town hall, which is worth planning a trip around.
la-orotava.getting: Ten minutes uphill from Puerto de la Cruz, or about forty minutes from Santa Cruz. From the southern resorts allow an hour and a quarter. The TF-21 continues up from here towards Teide, so it works well as a stop on the way. Park at the edge and walk in; the old streets are narrow and steep.
la-orotava.tips: Wear shoes you can walk uphill in — the gradient is real. Many shops still close for a long lunch. Combine it with Puerto de la Cruz below or with a drive up to Teide above, since it sits on the road between the two.
highlights: On the road up to Teide
faq: Is La Orotava worth visiting?
Yes, particularly if you like historic architecture. It is the best-preserved old town in the north and takes a couple of hours, easily combined with Puerto de la Cruz or a trip up to Teide.
When are the sand carpets in La Orotava?
They are laid for Corpus Christi, which falls in late spring or early summer depending on the year. Check the local dates before planning around it.

playa-el-bollullo.name: Playa El Bollullo
playa-el-bollullo.alt: The black sand and turquoise water of Playa El Bollullo
playa-el-bollullo.tagline: A black-sand cove below the banana terraces east of Puerto de la Cruz, and the north's prettiest beach.
playa-el-bollullo.intro: El Bollullo is a small cove of jet-black volcanic sand backed by cliffs and banana plantations, a few kilometres east of Puerto de la Cruz. The contrast of black sand against turquoise water makes it the most photographed beach in the north, and the short walk down keeps the crowds smaller than the numbers would suggest.
playa-el-bollullo.see: The beach, the cliffs and the water. There is a beach bar at the top of the path and little else, which is the appeal. Neighbouring coves — El Rincón and Los Patos — are reachable on foot along the shore at low tide, though this requires care and local advice about conditions. Surfers use this stretch when the swell is right.
playa-el-bollullo.getting: Park at the end of the track from La Quinta, east of Puerto de la Cruz, and walk down a stepped path of five to ten minutes. The car park is small and fills at weekends. There is no direct bus, so a car or a taxi from Puerto de la Cruz is realistic.
playa-el-bollullo.tips: This is an open Atlantic beach with real waves, currents and no lifeguard cover — swim with caution and get out if it is heavy. Black sand becomes genuinely hot underfoot in the middle of the day, so bring something for your feet. There is no shade, and the path back up is steeper than it looked on the way down.
highlights: Beach bar at the top of the path
faq: Can you swim at El Bollullo?
With caution. It is an open Atlantic beach with waves and currents and no lifeguards. Many visitors come for the setting and paddle rather than swim properly.
How do you get down to El Bollullo?
A stepped path of five to ten minutes from the small car park at the end of the track from La Quinta. There is no road access to the sand itself.

vilaflor.name: Vilaflor
vilaflor.alt: The village of Vilaflor among Canary pines
vilaflor.title: Vilaflor, Tenerife — Village Guide & Walks
vilaflor.tagline: The island's highest village, in the pine belt on the road up to Teide.
vilaflor.intro: Vilaflor de Chasna sits at roughly 1,400 metres on the southern slope, in the Canary pine forest between the resorts and the national park. It is the highest village in Tenerife and the last real settlement before the road climbs into the crater. Cool air, pine scent and terraced hillsides make it feel a long way from the coast it looks down on.
vilaflor.see: The village is small and takes an hour: a whitewashed church, steep lanes, terraces and viewpoints back down to the sea. What people really come for is what surrounds it. The Paisaje Lunar, the lunar landscape, is a set of pale eroded pumice pinnacles reached on a demanding walk of several hours, and it is one of the strangest sights on the island. Closer in, the Pino Gordo is among the largest Canary pines anywhere. Vilaflor is also the birthplace of Pedro de San José Betancur, born here in 1626 and canonised in 2002 as the first Canarian saint.
vilaflor.getting: About forty minutes up the TF-21 from Los Cristianos, on the main southern route to Teide, so it works naturally as a stop on the way up or down. TITSA line 482 links it with Los Cristianos. Parking in the village is limited to a few small areas.
vilaflor.tips: Bring a layer. At this altitude it is several degrees cooler than the coast and evenings are genuinely cold, which is exactly why islanders come up here in August. The Paisaje Lunar walk is long, exposed and poorly shaded — take water, start early and do not attempt it casually. You will see Vilaflor described as the highest village in Spain; that claim is often repeated but contested, since villages in mainland Andalucía sit higher.
highlights: Canary pine forest and the Pino Gordo
On the southern road to Teide
faq: Is Vilaflor the highest village in Spain?
It is the highest in Tenerife, at around 1,400 metres. The frequently repeated claim that it is the highest in Spain is contested, as some mainland villages sit higher.
Is the Paisaje Lunar walk hard?
Yes. It is several hours, exposed, and climbs a good deal. Take plenty of water, start early and treat it as a proper hike rather than a stroll.
Is Vilaflor worth stopping at on the way to Teide?
Yes. It breaks the climb, it is the last village before the park, and the pine forest around it is a different island from the coast.

playa-san-juan.name: Playa San Juan
playa-san-juan.alt: The harbour and town of Playa San Juan with La Gomera beyond
playa-san-juan.tagline: A working coastal town on the west coast, quiet, Canarian and largely undiscovered by the resorts.
playa-san-juan.intro: Playa San Juan sits on the west coast in the municipality of Guía de Isora, a former fishing and tomato-export port that has grown into a low-key town rather than a resort. There is a harbour, a dark-sand beach, a seafront promenade and very little that exists purely for visitors, which is exactly why people who find it tend to come back.
playa-san-juan.see: The beach and the harbour are the centre of it. The sand is dark and the water is usually calmer than the coast further north, and there is a promenade with unfussy restaurants where the prices are noticeably below Costa Adeje. La Gomera sits on the horizon and the sunsets from here are among the best on the island. There are no attractions as such; the point is a slow day.
playa-san-juan.getting: Roughly thirty minutes north of Costa Adeje on the TF-47, and about forty-five minutes from Tenerife South Airport. TITSA buses run along this coast between Los Cristianos and Los Gigantes. Parking is straightforward outside peak weekends.
playa-san-juan.tips: Come for the quiet rather than for things to do. It suits couples, walkers and anyone who wants a Canarian town with a beach attached rather than a resort. The west coast faces the sunset, so evening is the time to be on the front. There are some very smart hotels on the hillside above this stretch, which means the town has better restaurants than its size suggests.
highlights: Quiet working town, not a resort
faq: Is Playa San Juan a good place to stay?
For quiet, yes. It suits couples and older visitors who want a real town, good food and a beach, without nightlife or crowds. Anyone wanting resort facilities should look at Costa Adeje.
Can you swim at Playa San Juan?
Usually. The bay is more sheltered than much of the west coast, though this is still the open Atlantic — follow the flags.

alcala.name: Alcalá
alcala.alt: The natural sea pool at Alcalá
alcala.tagline: A small west-coast village built around a plaza and a natural sea pool.
alcala.intro: Alcalá is a few minutes north of Playa San Juan and smaller again: a plaza, a handful of streets, a little harbour and a natural seawater pool cut into the volcanic rock. Almost nothing here was built for tourism, and the village keeps the unhurried rhythm of somewhere that never expected visitors.
alcala.see: The natural pool is the reason to stop. Sheltered from the swell by the rock, it is swimmable on calm days and is where local families spend a Sunday. The plaza above it is the social centre, ringed by cafés, and there is a small beach and a coastal path linking the village with Playa San Juan. The Wednesday market is worth timing a visit around.
alcala.getting: About thirty-five minutes north of Costa Adeje on the TF-47, five minutes beyond Playa San Juan. TITSA buses on the west coast route stop here. Parking near the plaza is easy except on market day.
alcala.tips: The pool depends entirely on the sea state — excellent on a calm day, dangerous and best left alone when the swell is up, as anywhere on this coast. Alcalá has no resort infrastructure, so it is a half-day or an evening rather than a base for most visitors, though it makes a very peaceful one for anyone who wants nothing to happen.
highlights: Coastal path to Playa San Juan
faq: Can you swim in the natural pool at Alcalá?
On calm days, yes, and it is popular with local families. When the Atlantic swell is up it becomes dangerous and should be avoided.
Is Alcalá worth visiting?
If you want a Canarian village with no tourism built into it, yes. It is a half-day at most, and pairs naturally with Playa San Juan five minutes down the coast.
